cards.q: What is the DOM?
cards.a: It is the live object tree the browser builds when it parses your HTML, and exposes to JavaScript. It is not the HTML — that's a string, parsed once and then irrelevant — and it is not the pixels. It sits between them. Every node is a real JavaScript object you can read and mutate, and mutating it is what eventually causes a redraw.

cards.q: What's the difference between innerHTML and textContent?
cards.a: innerHTML runs your string through the HTML parser and builds real nodes from it. textContent treats the string as literal characters. So innerHTML with untrusted input is an XSS vulnerability, and textContent cannot be. I default to textContent and only reach for innerHTML for markup I authored.

cards.q: What is event bubbling?
cards.a: An event doesn't fire on one element — it travels a path. First capture, from the document down to the target; then the target itself; then bubbling, back up to the root. Listeners are registered for the bubble phase by default. Bubbling is what makes event delegation possible.

cards.q: What is event delegation and why would you use it?
cards.a: Instead of a listener per child, you put one listener on a common ancestor and inspect the event to work out which descendant it concerns. Two reasons: it replaces hundreds of listeners with one, and it automatically covers elements added later, because the listener was never attached to the children in the first place.

cards.q: What's the difference between e.target and e.currentTarget?
cards.a: e.target is where the event originated — the deepest element that was actually hit — and it never changes as the event travels. e.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running right now. In a delegated handler, currentTarget is the container and target might be an icon inside a button, which is why you use e.target.closest(...).

cards.q: What's the difference between preventDefault and stopPropagation?
cards.a: They're completely independent. preventDefault cancels the browser's built-in behaviour — navigating, submitting, moving focus. stopPropagation stops the event travelling to other elements. Cancelling a form submit needs preventDefault; stopPropagation would do nothing and would break any delegated listener above you.

cards.q: What's the difference between DOMContentLoaded and load?
cards.a: DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is parsed and deferred scripts have run — the tree is complete. load waits for every subresource, including images and iframes, which can be seconds later. Interface code wants DOMContentLoaded; waiting for load is a common and pointless delay.

cards.q: What's the difference between querySelectorAll and getElementsByClassName?
cards.a: querySelectorAll takes any CSS selector and returns a static NodeList — a snapshot. getElementsByClassName takes one class name and returns a live HTMLCollection, which changes underneath you as the document changes. The live one is the source of the classic infinite loop where you append inside an index-based loop over the collection.

cards.q: How do you create an element and add it to the page?
cards.a: document.createElement('div') gives you a real node that isn't in the document — no parent, no space, invisible. You configure it, then insert it with parent.append(el) or one of prepend/before/after. Splitting construction from insertion is deliberate: you build the whole subtree before anything is visible.

cards.q: Why does document.getElementById return null in my script?
cards.a: Almost always timing, not the selector. A classic <script> blocks the parser, so a script in <head> runs before <body> exists. Fix it with defer, type="module", or by putting the script at the end of <body>.

cards.q: What is the difference between an attribute and a property?
cards.a: The attribute is what was written in the HTML; the property is a field on the JavaScript object. They're two storage locations the browser keeps loosely in sync, with non-uniform rules. Attributes are always strings; properties have real types. And some deliberately diverge — input.value is the live value, while the value attribute is only the initial one.

cards.q: Why does input.value disagree with input.getAttribute('value')?
cards.a: Because the attribute is defined as the initial value, not the current one. Once the user types, the property tracks what they typed and the attribute still says what the HTML said. That's also why defaultValue exists — it's the property-side name for the attribute — and it's exactly the mechanism behind React's controlled vs uncontrolled inputs.

cards.q: What is layout thrashing?
cards.a: Interleaving DOM reads and writes in a loop. The browser normally batches writes and runs style/layout/paint once. But reading geometry — getBoundingClientRect, offsetHeight, scrollTop, getComputedStyle — while changes are pending forces layout immediately so it can answer truthfully. In a loop, that's N full layouts instead of one. The fix is to batch: read everything, then write everything.

cards.q: Why is animating transform better than animating left?
cards.a: left changes the box's position, so every frame re-runs layout and paint. transform and opacity can usually be handled entirely by the compositor, skipping layout and paint. At 60Hz you have about 16.7ms per frame, so which pipeline stages you trigger decides whether it's smooth.

cards.q: How would you handle clicks on a table with 500 rows?
cards.a: One delegated listener on the table. In the handler, e.target.closest('button.delete') to find the meaningful element, bail if there's no match, then act. One listener instead of 500, and rows added later work with no extra wiring.

cards.q: How do you remove an event listener you added with an arrow function?
cards.a: You can't — removeEventListener matches by function identity, and a second arrow expression is a different object, so it silently removes nothing. Either keep a named reference, or use an AbortController and pass { signal } to addEventListener, then call abort() to remove everything at once.

cards.q: What is IntersectionObserver and what does it replace?
cards.a: It tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport, at thresholds you choose, with the detection work happening inside the browser. It replaces the whole genre of scroll handlers that called getBoundingClientRect on every element — which is layout thrashing on every scroll event. Lazy loading, infinite scroll, scroll-spy nav and impression tracking are all one-liners with it.

cards.q: What's the difference between the input and change events?
cards.a: input fires on every change to the value as it happens. change fires when the value is committed — on blur for text fields, immediately for checkboxes, radios and selects. Live search wants input; a save-on-commit form wants change.

cards.q: Why shouldn't you use keydown to track what's in a text field?
cards.a: It doesn't reliably correspond to the value. Some keys produce no character, an IME can produce one character from several presses, and a paste or drag produces text with no key press at all. If you care about the value, listen to input. If you care about the key — a shortcut — listen to keydown.

cards.q: What's wrong with el.innerHTML += '<li>new</li>'?
cards.a: It serialises everything already in there to a string, concatenates, and reparses the whole subtree from scratch. Every existing node is destroyed and rebuilt, which silently drops every event listener, every bit of form state, and every node reference you were holding. Use append or insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', ...).

cards.q: How do you scroll an element into view?
cards.a: el.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'nearest' }). It does the arithmetic and handles nested scroll containers, which manual scrollTop maths gets wrong the moment there's more than one scrolling ancestor.

cards.q: How do you detect that a user has scrolled to the bottom of a list?
cards.a: el.scrollHeight - el.scrollTop - el.clientHeight approaching zero. But in practice I'd use an IntersectionObserver on a sentinel element at the end of the list — no scroll handler, no per-event measurement, and it handles the case where the list is shorter than the viewport.

cards.q: What does element.closest() do and why is it important?
cards.a: It walks upward from an element through its ancestors, including itself, and returns the first one matching a CSS selector. It's the inverse of querySelector. It matters because it's what makes event delegation robust — e.target is whatever pixel was hit, often an icon inside a button, and closest gets you to the element you actually meant.

cards.q: What's a DocumentFragment for?
cards.a: It's a lightweight parentless container. You append a thousand rows into it, then append the fragment once and it dissolves, delivering all its children in a single document mutation. It's the standard way to build a large list without touching the live document repeatedly.

cards.q: What's the difference between childNodes and children?
cards.a: childNodes includes text and comment nodes, so any whitespace in your markup shows up in it. children is elements only. Nearly every 'why is firstChild not my element' bug is this — the newline between your tags is a real text node.

cards.q: What is a MutationObserver and when would you actually use one?
cards.a: It reports changes to the DOM tree itself — nodes added or removed, attributes changed, text modified — asynchronously and in batches. In application code it's a last resort, usually when you need to react to a third-party script's changes to the page. In browser extensions and tooling it's everywhere.

cards.q: What replaced Mutation Events and why?
cards.a: MutationObserver, in Chrome 18 in 2012. Mutation Events were a DOM Level 2 feature deprecated in 2011 because they fired synchronously on every single change, which could make a page an order of magnitude slower. The observer batches and delivers asynchronously.

cards.q: What is Shadow DOM?
cards.a: A second, separate tree attached to an element via attachShadow. Nodes inside render in the element's place but are invisible to outside selectors, and styles don't cross the boundary in either direction — except inherited properties and CSS custom properties, which pass through deliberately and are the theming mechanism.

cards.q: What are custom elements?
cards.a: Tags you register with customElements.define('user-card', class extends HTMLElement {...}) that the parser and every DOM API treat as first-class elements. The name must have a hyphen so it can't collide with a future standard tag. You get lifecycle callbacks: connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, attributeChangedCallback, adoptedCallback.

cards.q: What is a Range?
cards.a: A pair of boundary points in the tree — start node plus offset, end node plus offset — describing a contiguous stretch of content that can cross element boundaries. It's the DOM's model of 'from here to there', and it's what window.getSelection() gives you access to.

cards.q: What does passive: true on a listener do?
cards.a: It promises the handler won't call preventDefault. Without that promise, the browser has to wait for your touchstart or wheel handler to finish before it knows whether it's allowed to scroll — so a slow handler stalls scrolling itself. It mattered enough that Chrome 56 in January 2017 made those listeners passive by default on document.

cards.q: What is the accessibility tree?
cards.a: A parallel tree the browser derives from the DOM, exposing each node's role, name, value and state to assistive technology through the OS. A screen reader reads that, not your CSS. Native elements populate it correctly for free; a <div onclick> populates none of it.

cards.q: What does getComputedStyle give you that element.style doesn't?
cards.a: element.style only reads the inline style attribute — if the value came from a stylesheet it's an empty string. getComputedStyle returns the value actually in effect after the full cascade and inheritance. It's also not free to call, because it may need layout to be current.

cards.q: What is ResizeObserver for?
cards.a: Knowing when a specific element changes size, for any reason — window resize, a sibling growing, content changing, a CSS change. Before it existed in Chrome 64 in 2018 there was no way to know an element resized unless the window did, which made component-level responsive behaviour genuinely impossible.

cards.q: How do you fire your own event between unrelated parts of a page?
cards.a: new CustomEvent('cart:updated', { detail: {...}, bubbles: true }) then el.dispatchEvent(e). The payload goes in detail. It lets one part of the page announce something without holding a reference to whoever's listening.

cards.q: A click handler on a button inside a card stopped working after you added a click handler on the card. What happened?
cards.a: Most likely the card's handler calls stopPropagation, or the card handler runs first in capture phase and removes/re-renders the button. Check for stopPropagation first — it's the usual culprit, and it also breaks analytics and any dropdown-close handler higher up. Usually the fix is to check e.target.closest() in the card handler and bail rather than stopping propagation.

cards.q: Your list re-renders and all the click handlers are gone. Why?
cards.a: Something is rebuilding the markup with innerHTML, which destroys and recreates every node — and listeners live on nodes, not on markup. Two fixes: use event delegation so the listener is on a stable ancestor, or stop rebuilding with innerHTML and mutate the existing nodes.

cards.q: A single-page app's memory grows every time the user navigates between views. How do you diagnose it?
cards.a: Chrome DevTools → Memory → Heap snapshot, filter for Detached, and compare snapshots across repeated mount/unmount cycles. Detached nodes that survive mean something still references them. The usual four: a listener on window or document, an observer never disconnected, an uncleared setInterval, or a cache holding node references.

cards.q: A scroll-driven animation stutters badly on a mid-range phone. What do you check?
cards.a: First whether the scroll handler measures anything — getBoundingClientRect or offsetTop inside a scroll handler forces layout on every event. Replace it with IntersectionObserver. Second, what's being animated — if it's top/left/width, every frame re-runs layout; move to transform. Third, whether the handler is passive.

cards.q: A user reports that pasting into your search box doesn't trigger the search. What's the bug?
cards.a: You're listening to keydown or keyup. A paste produces no key press. Listen to input, which fires for any change to the value regardless of how it got there — typing, pasting, dragging, autofill, or IME composition.

cards.q: A drag-and-drop implementation never fires drop. What's missing?
cards.a: e.preventDefault() in the dragover handler. Without it the browser's default is to reject the drop, so drop never fires. It's the single most common HTML5 drag-and-drop gotcha.

cards.q: Your modal opens but keyboard users can still tab into the page behind it. How do you fix it properly?
cards.a: Use <dialog> with showModal(), which handles focus movement, inerting the background, the top layer and the Escape key natively. If you can't, move focus into the dialog on open, apply inert to the rest of the page, trap Tab inside, and return focus to the trigger on close.

cards.q: Something on the page is being modified by a third-party script and breaking your layout. How do you respond?
cards.a: A MutationObserver scoped to the affected subtree, so you can detect and correct the change. It's genuinely the right tool here — this is the case it exists for, because you don't control the code doing the mutating and can't hook it directly.

cards.q: A form submits and reloads the page despite your fetch call. Why?
cards.a: You didn't call e.preventDefault() in the submit handler, or you returned early before reaching it. Native submission is the default action; the fetch runs and then the page navigates away and discards it.

cards.q: You call removeEventListener and the handler still fires. What are the two likely causes?
cards.a: Either you passed a different function reference than the one you added — an inline arrow, or a .bind(this) which creates a new function every call — or the capture setting doesn't match. Add and remove must agree on both identity and phase.

cards.q: Your DOMContentLoaded handler never runs. What's the likely cause?
cards.a: You registered it after the event already fired — for example from a dynamically imported module or a late-loading async script. Guard it: if (document.readyState === 'loading') addEventListener(...); else init();

cards.q: When would you use innerHTML rather than building nodes?
cards.a: When the markup is authored by me and static, and I'm setting a whole subtree at once — it's genuinely more readable and the parser is fast. I would not use it for anything containing a value from a user, a database or an API. If untrusted HTML must be rendered, it goes through DOMPurify first.

cards.q: Event delegation versus per-element listeners — when is delegation the wrong choice?
cards.a: When the elements are few and stable, delegation adds indirection for nothing. It's also awkward for events that don't bubble — focus, blur, mouseenter — though focusin/focusout cover the focus case. And a delegated handler runs for every event in the region, so if the region is huge and the handler is expensive, that's a real cost.

cards.q: Would you use Web Components on a new project?
cards.a: For a design system consumed by teams using different frameworks, or widgets embedded in pages I don't control — yes, that's exactly what they're for. For a normal product app where the team already has React — no. The framework's component model is more ergonomic, and shadow boundaries complicate global styling, form participation and server rendering. They're used far less than their promise suggested, and that's why.

cards.q: getBoundingClientRect versus offsetTop/offsetWidth — which and why?
cards.a: getBoundingClientRect almost always. It's viewport-relative, gives sub-pixel floats, and accounts for transforms. The offset* family gives integers and is relative to offsetParent, which is whatever the nearest positioned ancestor happens to be — so the meaning changes when someone adds position: relative somewhere unrelated.

cards.q: When is a scroll event listener still the right tool over IntersectionObserver?
cards.a: When you need continuous scroll position rather than a threshold crossing — a progress bar, a parallax offset, a header that shrinks proportionally. Then you read window.scrollY, which is cheap, coalesce into requestAnimationFrame, and never measure elements inside the handler.

cards.q: Why would you choose a framework over plain DOM manipulation?
cards.a: Because hand-writing the bridge between state and DOM means writing a specific mutation sequence for every possible state transition, and transitions grow much faster than states. Miss one and the screen disagrees with the data. A framework lets you write a function from state to a description of the tree and computes the mutations. That's the only thing it takes over — events, geometry, focus, accessibility and teardown are all still yours.

cards.q: textContent versus innerText — which do you reach for?
cards.a: textContent, unless I specifically need what's rendered. innerText respects display: none, collapses whitespace the way CSS does, and inserts breaks at block boundaries — which means the browser may have to run layout to answer, so it can be expensive. textContent is answerable from the tree alone.

cards.q: Shadow DOM open versus closed mode?
cards.a: Open, almost always. Closed only hides el.shadowRoot from outside code — it is not a security boundary, anyone can still reach in by patching attachShadow, and it makes testing and debugging harder for no real gain.

cards.q: defer versus async versus script at the end of body?
cards.a: defer or a module for anything touching the DOM: parallel download, executes after parsing, and multiple deferred scripts keep document order. async only for genuinely independent things like analytics, because execution time and order are unpredictable. End-of-body still works and is what you use when you can't change the tag attributes.

cards.q: Walk me through how you'd build a searchable, sortable table without a framework.
cards.a: Render rows once from data into a DocumentFragment and append it in one mutation. One delegated click listener on the <thead> for sorting, using closest('th') and a data-sort-key attribute to know which column. One input listener on the search box, debounced. Sorting and filtering happen on the data array, then I re-render — and because the listeners are delegated to stable ancestors, re-rendering doesn't lose them.

cards.q: How would you implement infinite scroll?
cards.a: A sentinel element after the last row and an IntersectionObserver watching it with a rootMargin so it fires a few hundred pixels early. When it intersects, fetch the next page, append rows via a fragment, and leave the sentinel at the end. No scroll handler, no per-event measurement, and it correctly handles the case where the first page doesn't fill the viewport.

cards.q: How would you build an accessible dropdown menu?
cards.a: Native <button> as the trigger with aria-expanded kept in sync with the open state, and aria-controls pointing at the menu. Arrow keys move focus between items, Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger, Tab closes. A delegated click on the menu handles selection. A document click listener closes on outside click — and it checks e.target.closest() rather than the menu calling stopPropagation, which would break everything else on the page.

cards.q: You built qbank with Fastify and a React front end. Where does the DOM actually show up in that stack?
cards.a: Everywhere React touches the screen, and in the places React deliberately doesn't. React replaces the node-building layer only. The synthetic event system is delegation. useRef exists because measurement, focus and third-party integration need a real node. useEffect cleanup is listener and observer teardown. And layout thrashing and accessibility aren't handled by React at all — if a component reads getBoundingClientRect during render, that forces layout exactly as plain DOM code would.

cards.q: Describe a DOM performance problem you'd expect to find in a vibe-coded app.
cards.a: Reads and writes interleaved in a loop — something like measuring each item's height and setting a style from it in the same iteration, which forces a full layout per item. Also scroll handlers that measure elements instead of using IntersectionObserver, and innerHTML += in a loop, which rebuilds the entire subtree every iteration and destroys listeners along the way.

cards.q: How would you audit an existing page for DOM-based XSS?
cards.a: Find the sinks first — every assignment to innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, and any eval-adjacent call. Then trace backwards to see whether any value reaching them originates from location, a query parameter, postMessage, or an API response. Anything that does gets switched to textContent, rebuilt with createElement, or routed through DOMPurify. Then a CSP without 'unsafe-inline' as defence in depth.

cards.q: How do you decide between a native element and a custom widget?
cards.a: Native first, always. <button>, <dialog>, <details>, <select> come with role, focus behaviour, keyboard activation and screen-reader naming for free, and reimplementing that correctly is a lot of work that's easy to get subtly wrong. I only build a custom widget when the native one genuinely can't be styled or behave the way the design requires, and then I accept that the ARIA and focus management are now my job.

cards.q: Why does the DOM exist at all?
cards.a: Because before it, a page was a finished document — every change meant asking the server for a whole new one, over a modem, discarding everything on screen. The browser already had a parsed structure internally; the DOM is that structure made addressable from a program. DOM Level 1 in October 1998 was the point where that became one standard rather than IE's document.all versus Netscape's document.layers.

cards.q: Why do both capture and bubble phases exist?
cards.a: Netscape and Microsoft implemented opposite propagation models during the browser wars. DOM Level 2 Events in November 2000 resolved the argument by specifying both and letting the developer pick with the capture option. It's a compatibility artefact that turned out to be genuinely useful.

cards.q: Why did addEventListener replace el.onclick?
cards.a: Because onclick is a single slot — assigning twice silently replaces the first handler, so two independent pieces of code can't both listen to the same event on the same element. That's untenable the moment a page contains more than one author's work. Inline onclick attributes have the extra problem of being strings evaluated in global scope, which CSP exists to forbid.

cards.q: Why is whitespace between tags a text node?
cards.a: Because the DOM models documents in general, not just application UI, and in a document the text between elements is the content. The parser can't know your newlines are formatting rather than meaningful. That's why the element-only traversal properties — children, firstElementChild, nextElementSibling — were added alongside the original node-level ones.

cards.q: Why does cloneNode not copy event listeners?
cards.a: Because listeners aren't part of the node's data — they're a separate registration held by the event system, keyed on the node. The clone is a new node with the same attributes and children, and nothing has registered anything against it.

cards.q: Why can't a node be in two places at once?
cards.a: Because the DOM is a tree and a tree node has exactly one parent. So there's no insertion operation that duplicates — inserting a node that's already in the document moves it. If you want a copy you ask for one explicitly with cloneNode. This is also why React needs key: the diffing algorithm has to know node identity to decide what to move versus recreate.

cards.q: Why does a classic script block the HTML parser?
cards.a: Because of document.write — a script was historically allowed to inject markup at its own position in the token stream, so the parser couldn't safely continue past it. defer and modules exist to opt out of that guarantee, which is why they can download in parallel and execute after parsing.

cards.q: Why did Trusted Types get invented when we already had CSP and sanitisers?
cards.a: Because CSP restricts what can execute but doesn't stop a dangerous assignment, and sanitisers only help where someone remembered to call them. Trusted Types makes assigning a plain string to innerHTML throw, so the dangerous sinks structurally cannot be fed unvetted values. It moves the guarantee from discipline to enforcement. Chrome 83 in 2020, still Chromium-only.

cards.q: Walk me through what the browser does between a DOM mutation and a pixel changing.
cards.a: Style — recompute which CSS rules apply to which elements. Layout, sometimes called reflow — compute position and size of every affected box. Paint — fill in pixels per layer. Composite — assemble layers into the final frame. The browser batches mutations and normally runs this once before the next paint, which is why individual writes are cheap and forcing the pipeline mid-loop is not.

cards.q: Which property reads force a synchronous layout, and why those?
cards.a: getBoundingClientRect, the offset*, client* and scroll* metrics, getComputedStyle, and innerText. They all require a truthful answer about geometry or rendered output, which the browser can't give from stale data while mutations are queued — so it runs layout immediately.

cards.q: How does event retargeting work at a shadow boundary?
cards.a: An event crossing out of a shadow tree has its target rewritten to the host element rather than the internal node, so outside code can't learn the shadow tree's internal structure from an event. e.composedPath() gives you the full path when you legitimately need it.

cards.q: What does the HTML parser do with malformed markup, and why does that matter?
cards.a: It repairs it, by specification — closing unclosed tags, relocating a stray element out of a table, dropping a <p> nested in a <p>. It matters because the tree you get is the repaired one, so outerHTML gives you the serialisation of the repair rather than what you wrote, and innerHTML parsing is context-sensitive — a <tr> string assigned to a <div> has its tags discarded.

cards.q: How does AbortController integrate with event listeners?
cards.a: addEventListener gained a signal option in Chrome 90, April 2021. You pass { signal: controller.signal } on every listener a component registers, and one controller.abort() removes all of them — no need to keep function references purely so removeEventListener can match by identity. The same controller also cancels in-flight fetch calls.

cards.q: Explain the ResizeObserver loop error.
cards.a: The callback runs at a defined point in the frame lifecycle. If a callback resizes the element it observes, that schedules another callback, which resizes again — a cycle. The browser detects it and reports 'ResizeObserver loop limit exceeded' rather than hanging. Usually it means the callback is writing a dimension it's also reading.

cards.q: How would you build a virtual DOM diff, conceptually?
cards.a: Build a plain-object tree describing the desired output — cheap, no DOM involved. Compare it against the previous description node by node. Same type at the same position means patch attributes and recurse into children; different type means replace the subtree. For lists you need stable identity to avoid recreating everything on reorder, which is what a key supplies. The output is a minimal sequence of real DOM operations, applied in one pass.

cards.q: What's the difference between the visual viewport and the layout viewport?
cards.a: The layout viewport is what CSS lays out against. The visual viewport is what's actually visible, which on mobile changes when the on-screen keyboard appears or the user pinch-zooms. The visualViewport object reports the latter, and it's what you need for positioning something relative to what the user can genuinely see.

cards.q: Where should a script tag go and with what attributes?
cards.a: <script defer src="..."> in the head, or type="module", which is deferred by default. Both download in parallel with parsing and execute after the tree is complete, and deferred scripts keep document order. async only for independent scripts like analytics.

cards.q: How do you safely initialise code that must run once the DOM is ready?
cards.a: if (document.readyState === 'loading') { document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init); } else { init(); } — because a listener registered after the event already fired never runs, which happens with dynamically imported modules.

cards.q: How do you set and read a CSS custom property from JavaScript?
cards.a: el.style.setProperty('--accent', 'tomato') to set, and getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue('--accent') to read. Custom properties keep their literal names — they are not camelCased like standard properties on el.style.

cards.q: What CSP directive most directly reduces XSS risk, and what does it break?
cards.a: A script-src without 'unsafe-inline'. It breaks inline <script> blocks and every onclick="..." attribute, which is the point — those are the injection sinks. You move to external scripts and addEventListener, or use nonces or hashes for the inline blocks you genuinely need.

cards.q: How do you observe only attribute changes on a subtree?
cards.a: observer.observe(root, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['class', 'data-state'], subtree: true }). The filter matters — observing all attributes on a large subtree produces a lot of records you then have to discard.

cards.q: What happens if you assign a <tr> string to a <div>'s innerHTML?
cards.a: The tags are discarded and you're left with the text content. HTML parsing is context-sensitive — a table row is only valid inside a table section, so the parser drops it. This is why <template> or DOMParser is safer for parsing arbitrary fragments.

cards.q: Does a <script> inserted via innerHTML run?
cards.a: No — the HTML spec explicitly disables it. And it buys you almost nothing, because <img src=x onerror=...>, <svg onload=...> and <iframe srcdoc=...> all work. Treat innerHTML with untrusted input as executing that input.

cards.q: Can you preventDefault a scroll event?
cards.a: No — scroll has cancelable: false; by the time it fires the scroll has happened. You prevent it at the source, on wheel or touchmove with a non-passive listener, or with CSS overflow: hidden / overscroll-behavior.

cards.q: What's parentNode versus parentElement for the <html> element?
cards.a: parentNode is the document node; parentElement is null, because the document isn't an element. That's the only place the two disagree, and it's why a loop climbing with parentElement terminates cleanly while one using parentNode needs a guard.

cards.q: Why does el.href not match the string in the markup?
cards.a: The href attribute reflects into the property as a fully resolved absolute URL. href="/docs" reads back as https://example.com/docs. Comparing el.href to a relative path never matches — use getAttribute('href') for the literal value.

cards.q: What does setAttribute('disabled', false) do?
cards.a: Disables the element. The attribute becomes the string "false", and HTML boolean attributes are true whenever present regardless of value. Use the property, el.disabled = false, or removeAttribute('disabled').

cards.q: Which events don't bubble, and what do you do about it?
cards.a: focus, blur, load, error, element scroll, and mouseenter/mouseleave. For focus, use focusin/focusout, which are the bubbling equivalents and exist specifically for delegation. For the others, attach directly or use capture phase, which reaches the element on the way down.

cards.q: What happens when you iterate a live HTMLCollection by index and append inside the loop?
cards.a: An infinite loop. The collection is a standing query, not a snapshot, so every appended match extends it — the collection grows exactly as fast as the index advances and length is never reached. Snapshot it first with Array.from(...).

cards.q: Is a.contains(a) true?
cards.a: Yes. contains treats a node as containing itself, and closest likewise includes the element itself in its upward walk. Both are convenient in delegation and occasionally surprising in loop conditions.

cards.q: Why might getBoundingClientRect return all zeros?
cards.a: The element isn't rendered — it's display: none, detached from the document, or inside a collapsed container. There's no box, so there are no coordinates. Note that visibility: hidden still produces a box and non-zero values.
